Josh: Ugh! I have been studying the For Loop in JavaScript since yesterday, but I don't really get it! I must be pretty dumb.
Drake: Don't be so harsh on yourself! It's not that hard. I've been working with JavaScript for a while now. Let me explain to you the easiest way.
Josh: Ok, thanks.
Drake: You know what looping is, right? Well, For Loop is the most compact form of looping. It only has 3 parts.

Josh: How can a looping form only have three parts?
Drake: Yes. It has been the most useful and practical tool. Besides, you know that the longer the code, the easier for bugs and glitches to appear. The first part of the For Loop is the loop initialization. A counter with a starting value is initialized.
Josh: And this happens before the loop begins, right?
Drake: Exactly! The second step is the test statement. It is called test because that's what it does; it tests or evaluates whether a given condition is true or not. If the statement is true, the code inside the loop will be executed. If it is false, the control will come out of the loop.

Josh: Oh, I get it now! I've had problems with that step, because I got confused with the true or false statement.
Drake: Yeah, when you start learning about JavaScript, the loop concept is hard to grasp. Anyways, the last step is the iteration statement; this is the easiest one, you use it to increase or decrease the counter value.
Josh: Oh, thanks! You've helped me a lot! Just one more question, how do you identify the syntax used in a For Loop?
Drake: When you have been into programming for so long, as I have, you learn that all the tree parts can be put in a single line separated by semicolons.

Present Perfect Simple vs Present Perfect Continuous
We use Present Perfect Simple and Present Perfect Continuous to talk about actions that started in the past but are still happening or can happen again.

We use Present perfect to talk about actions or experiences that started in the past but are still relevant in the present, we do not focus on the duration of the action

Structure
Subject + have/has + verb in past participle + complement

Examples
I have travelled to Canada twice.
Have you ever seen star wars?
She hasn't worked in two years, she is focused in taking care of her baby.

 We use present perfect continuous for actions that started in the past but are still happening at the moment and we want to focus on the duration of the action.

We use the following structure:
Subject + have/has been + verb-ing + complement

Examples:
I have been working in this company all my life.
She hasn't been studying Japanese for 5 years but only 3.
Have you been sleeping well lately?
